strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult vision/graphics problem: reconstructing real, high-frequency flame dynamics from only three commodity cameras. The focus on sparse-view real fire capture is distinctive and relevant for dynamic novel-view synthesis, simulation, robotics, and visual effects.

The proposed pipeline is technically sensible: separating static background reconstruction from dynamic fire, using stereo plus monocular depth priors for the static scene, and initializing FreeTimeGS-style dynamic Gaussians from fused multi-view optical flow directly targets the underconstrained nature of the problem.

The real capture system and dataset are a meaningful contribution. The hardware synchronization pattern using LEDs/rolling shutter is practical, low-cost, and described clearly enough to be useful for others attempting high-speed multi-camera capture.

Quantitative results over 17 real scenes show clear gains over two 4D Gaussian baselines on flame-region PSNR/SSIM and much lower pseudo-depth error. The qualitative comparisons also support the claim that generic dynamic Gaussian methods overfit sparse views and can produce degenerate geometry.
The supplementary material improves reproducibility by giving implementation details, compute requirements, per-scene tables, ablations, and a statement that code plus data will be released.
weaknesses: The evidence for true 3D/4D reconstruction remains incomplete. The main quantitative validation holds out every 8th frame from the same three camera views, so it primarily evaluates temporal interpolation/re-rendering at observed viewpoints rather than rigorous novel-view generalization. Since the paper claims arbitrary novel-view rendering and geometrically plausible reconstruction, a held-out camera, additional validation cameras, or controlled synthetic/physical ground truth would be much more convincing.

The depth metric is only a comparison to linearly aligned monocular depth predictions, not ground-truth geometry. This is especially problematic because monocular depth priors are also part of the pipeline for the static scene, and for transparent/emissive flames the monocular depth target is itself unreliable. The reported RMSE depth should therefore be interpreted as a weak plausibility proxy rather than strong geometric evidence.

The baseline comparison may not be fully fair or sufficient. The two 4DGS baselines are randomly initialized and use author-provided parameters for a different scene; one baseline also required an imposed Gaussian-count limit due to memory overflow. There is no direct comparison to FreeTimeGS with comparable depth/background initialization, no baseline that uses the same static/dynamic decomposition without flow initialization, and no comparison to fire/smoke-specific reconstruction or tomography-inspired methods where applicable.

Several claimed components are only weakly supported by the ablations. Disabling rolling-shutter modeling has essentially no quantitative effect, and the artificial NoSync perturbation causes only a small drop. RandomFlow is worse on average for flame SSIM but sometimes improves individual metrics/scenes, so the necessity and robustness of the fused 3D flow initialization are less clear than the narrative suggests.

The novelty is incremental at the algorithmic level: the method combines existing 3DGS, FreeTimeGS-style temporal Gaussians, optical flow, stereo/monocular depth priors, and synchronization hardware. The paper’s strongest contribution is arguably an applied/systems plus dataset contribution rather than a fundamentally new representation; judged as Algorithms/General, the technical novelty is moderate.

The method depends on several fragile assumptions: flames are brighter than the background for minimum-intensity fire removal, the background is mostly static and weakly affected by smoke/illumination, optical flow is meaningful for emissive turbulent fire, and linear per-Gaussian velocities are adequate over the chosen lifetime. The limitations mention these issues, but the experiments do not stress-test failures such as dense smoke, strong firelight flicker on the background, reflective scenes, or larger uncontrolled fires.

Reproducibility is promising but not yet complete in the submitted manuscript: the full dataset and complete codebase are stated as future public releases, while only a short example scene is included in the supplement. Important hyperparameters such as voxel resolution, masking/segmentation details, flow fusion settings, and synchronization extraction details could be specified more completely.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely difficult and visually important problem: sparse-view 4D reconstruction of real flames, which are emissive, transparent, fast, and geometrically ambiguous.

The proposed system is practically motivated. The three-camera GoPro setup, LED/rolling-shutter synchronization pattern, static/dynamic separation, depth-assisted background reconstruction, and flow-initialized dynamic Gaussians form a coherent applied pipeline.

The captured fire dataset appears useful, with 17 real sequences across propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper, and alcohol, recorded at 400 Hz. This is a valuable direction if the data and code are actually released.
The paper provides comparisons to two 4D Gaussian baselines and includes several ablations, plus per-scene supplementary tables, which helps diagnose which components matter.

The qualitative results suggest that the method can produce plausible renderings of flames from sparse synchronized videos, and the static/dynamic decomposition seems especially helpful for preventing background geometry collapse.
weaknesses: I assess this primarily as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. Under that lens, the system is interesting, but the evidence does not convincingly establish the claimed 3D/4D reconstruction fidelity.

The evaluation protocol is weak for the main claim of novel-view 3D reconstruction. The validation split removes every 8th frame from the same three camera views, so the main quantitative metrics largely test temporal interpolation/re-rendering at observed viewpoints rather than held-out-view generalization. The supplementary novel-view results are qualitative only.

The depth evaluation is not convincing. RMSE depth is computed against monocular Depth Anything V2 predictions after alignment, while monocular depth is also part of the reconstruction pipeline/regularization. This is not ground-truth geometry and risks being circular; it cannot validate flame geometry, especially for transparent/emissive regions where monocular depth is unreliable.

The central contribution of flow initialization is only modestly supported. The RandomFlow ablation is close to the full method in full-frame PSNR/LPIPS and sometimes better on individual scenes; the average masked fire PSNR drops only from 27.46 to 27.01. This undercuts the claim that fused 3D optical flow is a decisive component.

The rolling-shutter modeling and custom synchronization are emphasized as contributions, but the GlobalShutter ablation is essentially indistinguishable from the baseline, and NoSync produces only a small degradation. This makes the practical importance of these components unclear relative to the paper's claims.

The baselines may be disadvantaged. The paper uses author-provided parameters for a DyNeRF flame_salmonscene and random initialization for 4DGS baselines, while the proposed method benefits from strong task-specific preprocessing, depth initialization, static pretraining, masks, and flow. Stronger adapted baselines are needed, such as FreeTimeGS with the same static/dynamic split but random/no-flow velocities, depth-initialized 4DGS, or optimization with tuned hyperparameters.

The method appears highly engineered from existing components: COLMAP/PatchMatch stereo, Depth Anything V2, MEMFOF, vanilla 3DGS, and FreeTimeGS. The paper does not sufficiently separate what is novel from what is an integration of known tools, nor does it quantify the added value of each tool rigorously enough.

Claims about physically plausible motion and downstream interpretability of the velocity field are not validated. There is no comparison to measured flow, simulation, multi-view tomography, particle tracking, or any physical consistency criterion; the velocity field may simply be a rendering prior.

The dataset remains limited despite being useful: only three cameras, 100-frame reconstruction clips per scene, no ground-truth geometry, no true held-out camera, and no public release at submission time beyond a short example in supplementary material. This limits reproducibility and scientific verification.

The paper would benefit from stronger attribution and comparison to fire/smoke-specific reconstruction methods, including tomography and physics-informed approaches. These are cited, but not empirically compared or deeply discussed relative to the proposed setting.

There are clarity and polish issues, including typos and awkward phrasing in tables/text, inconsistent notation, and some overclaims such as 'microsecond-level synchronization' and 'physically plausible reconstructions' without corresponding quantitative evidence.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and genuinely difficult vision problem: reconstructing high-frequency, semi-transparent, emissive fire dynamics from only three consumer cameras. This is a valuable setting where standard dynamic view-synthesis assumptions are stressed.

The proposed system is coherent and well motivated. Separating static background reconstruction from dynamic fire reconstruction, using stereo plus monocular depth regularization for sparse-view geometry, and initializing FreeTimeGS-style dynamic Gaussians from fused optical flow are sensible design choices for this domain.

The capture contribution is practically useful. The LED/rolling-shutter synchronization setup is low-cost, well explained, and paired with a new real-world dataset covering 17 fire scenes with varied fuels and flame behaviors.

The experiments show clear gains in the fire regions over two 4DGS baselines: mean PSNRflame/SSIMflame improve over both baselines, and the reported depth-alignment errors suggest that the competing methods overfit image appearance while producing implausible geometry.

The paper includes meaningful ablations for static pretraining, flow initialization, synchronization, and rolling-shutter modeling, plus per-scene supplementary results and implementation details. The limitations section is candid about optical-flow errors, linear motion assumptions, and smoke/background interactions.
The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful pipeline diagrams and qualitative comparisons that make the technical idea easy to follow.
weaknesses: The main novelty is primarily a well-engineered pipeline combining existing components rather than a fundamentally new reconstruction model. This is still valuable as an Algorithms/General applied reconstruction contribution, but the scientific advance is more incremental than the presentation sometimes implies.

The evaluation lacks strong ground truth for 3D geometry or motion. RMSEdepth is measured against monocular depth predictions after alignment, and monocular depth is also part of the method's static-scene regularization pipeline, so this metric is only a weak proxy for geometric correctness.

The quantitative protocol mostly evaluates held-out frames from the same three camera views. For claims about novel-view synthesis and 3D reconstruction, a held-out camera or controlled synthetic/real setup with additional views would provide much stronger evidence.

The baseline comparison may not be fully fair or exhaustive. The 4DGS baselines are randomly initialized with author-provided settings for another scene, while the proposed method receives domain-specific initialization, masks, depth priors, synchronization, and static-scene preprocessing. More carefully tuned or similarly initialized baselines would strengthen the case.

Some claimed components appear to have limited measured impact. The rolling-shutter ablation is essentially tied with the full method, and the NoSync degradation is modest, which weakens the argument that these parts are central to the reconstruction quality despite their practical interest.

The method relies on several preprocessing assumptions and external predictors: dynamic-region segmentation, MEMFOF optical flow, DepthAnythingV2 depth, COLMAP/PatchMatchStereo, and background estimation by minimum intensity projection. Failure modes of these dependencies are discussed but not deeply quantified.

The dataset is useful but still modest for generalization claims: only 17 scenes, and only 100 synchronized frames per scene are used for reconstruction. The method's robustness to different camera baselines, lighting conditions, smoke-heavy fires, severe occlusions, and outdoor wind variation remains underexplored.

Reproducibility is promising because code and data are promised and supplementary details are provided, but the full dataset/code are not actually available in the manuscript package beyond a short example, so independent verification is not yet possible.

strengths: The paper targets an important and genuinely difficult vision/graphics problem: sparse-view 4D reconstruction of real flames, where standard persistent-primitive dynamic Gaussian methods are poorly matched to the phenomenon.

The proposed decomposition into static background reconstruction plus transient flame Gaussians with lifetime and velocity parameters is technically sensible and well motivated for emissive, non-rigid, short-lived structures.

The capture setup is a practical contribution: three high-speed consumer cameras, a low-cost LED/rolling-shutter synchronization scheme, and a dataset spanning 17 real fire scenes with varied fuels and backgrounds.

The evaluation is broader than simple image metrics: the paper reports masked flame PSNR/SSIM, LPIPS, pseudo-depth consistency, video quality, and synthetic velocity-field metrics, and compares against several relevant Gaussian-splatting baselines.
Results are consistently favorable to the proposed method, with clear gains over 4DGS, Grid4D, and FreeTimeGS in flame-region appearance and especially in synthetic motion-direction similarity.
The limitations section is honest about reliance on optical flow, constant-velocity motion, background/foreground separation assumptions, and synchronization error.
weaknesses: The real-world geometric evaluation is not fully convincing. Flame depth is compared to monocular depth predictions after alignment, while monocular depth is also used in the pipeline for static regularization; this is only a weak proxy for true 3D accuracy and does not establish physically correct flame geometry.

The main real-data validation appears to hold out every 8th frame rather than holding out camera viewpoints. This primarily tests temporal/image interpolation in observed views, while the paper makes strong claims about novel-view 4D reconstruction from sparse views.

The ablations weaken some claimed necessities. NoSync is almost identical to the full method on real metrics, and RandFlow changes real visual metrics only modestly, suggesting that the stated importance of synchronization and flow initialization is not fully demonstrated for the main real-world setting.

Baseline fairness is somewhat uncertain. Most baselines use author-provided settings for a different flame scene and are initialized from COLMAP points, while the proposed method receives specialized depth, motion masks, optical flow, and synchronization handling tailored to fire. Stronger tuning or adapted variants would make the comparison more decisive.

The synthetic motion evaluation is valuable but narrow: only three simulated scenes are used, and the DVE metric evaluates Gaussian velocities under the authors' density-weighted formulation. This supports motion plausibility but does not fully validate turbulent real-fire dynamics.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the code/data section says the official repository will be provided but the repository location is blank, and several implementation choices such as masks, voxel size, and preprocessing thresholds are only partially specified.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The method combines known components, including 3DGS, Depth Anything, PatchMatchStereo, MEMFOF, FreeTimeGS-like lifetime/velocity parameters, and motion masking; the novelty lies mostly in integration and adaptation to fire rather than a fundamentally new representation or optimizer.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and underexplored vision problem: sparse-view reconstruction of transient, emissive fire, where standard dynamic Gaussian splatting assumptions are plausibly brittle.
The system is practically motivated and reasonably complete, combining static/background reconstruction, flow-initialized transient Gaussians, masking losses, and a low-cost synchronization setup.
The authors evaluate on a nontrivial set of 17 real captured fire sequences and three synthetic fire simulations, and they include comparisons to several Gaussian-splatting baselines plus ablations.
The limitations section is candid about optical-flow errors, the restrictive linear-velocity model, foreground/background separation assumptions, and synchronization artifacts.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. Much of the method appears to be a task-specific composition of existing ingredients: vanilla 3DGS, stereo plus monocular depth regularization, optical-flow initialization, and FreeTimeGS-like lifetime/velocity parameters. The paper does not make a strong case that the formulation is fundamentally new rather than an engineering adaptation for flames.

The evaluation protocol is not fully convincing for the central claims. Real-scene validation holds out every 8th frame from the same three camera views, which mainly tests temporal interpolation/reconstruction in observed views rather than robust novel-view 4D reconstruction from sparse cameras.

The depth metric is weakly grounded: rendered flame depth is compared to monocular depth estimates after linear alignment, not to measured geometry. Since monocular depth priors are also part of the pipeline for the static scene, this does not provide strong independent evidence of correct 3D structure.

The baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns. The baselines use author-provided hyperparameters for a different DyNeRF flame scene, and FreeTimeGS uses an unofficial implementation. There is little evidence that baselines were carefully adapted to this sparse three-camera fire setting, so the reported large gaps may partly reflect tuning and initialization mismatch.

The synchronization contribution is undermined by the ablation: NoSync has almost identical real-image metrics to the full method, and only a small degradation on synthetic velocity metrics. This makes the custom hardware/synchronization component look less essential than claimed.

The proposed DVE motion metric is reasonable in spirit but is introduced and used by the authors themselves on only three synthetic scenes. It is not validated against perceptual or physical criteria, and the real-world experiments still lack ground-truth motion or geometry, leaving the physical-plausibility claims insufficiently supported.

Ablations are not consistently supportive. RandFlow remains close to the full method on real visual metrics, NoMask even improves several visual scores, and JointOpt slightly improves synthetic motion metrics. These results suggest the claimed components mainly trade off metrics rather than clearly contributing to a robust reconstruction solution.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the code/data section ends with an empty repository reference, and many implementation choices are only described at a high level. This is a significant issue for a complex capture-and-reconstruction pipeline.

The paper does not adequately test generalization. There is no camera-count ablation beyond the fixed three-view setup, no evaluation on truly held-out viewpoints in the quantitative tables, no comparison to relevant non-GS volumetric/fluid reconstruction methods despite making broad claims about fire reconstruction, and limited analysis of failure cases such as smoke-rich scenes, large flames, reflective backgrounds, or changing illumination.

Overall, the work has an appealing application and some useful system engineering, but the scientific case is not strong enough for acceptance: the novelty is incremental, the strongest claims rely on imperfect metrics, and the experimental design leaves substantial uncertainty about true 3D/4D reconstruction quality.

strengths: The paper tackles a clear and difficult computer vision/graphics problem: sparse-view reconstruction of highly dynamic, emissive, semi-transparent fire. The motivation is strong, and the authors convincingly explain why persistent-primitive dynamic Gaussian methods are poorly matched to flames.

The proposed pipeline is technically coherent and well targeted to the problem. Separating static background reconstruction from transient flame reconstruction, initializing dynamic Gaussians from fused multi-view optical flow, and assigning lifetime/velocity parameters to flame Gaussians are sensible design choices that address the key ambiguities of three-view fire capture.

The work has a valuable applied/systems component even though no contribution type is explicitly declared. In addition to the algorithmic formulation, the paper describes a practical high-speed three-camera capture setup with low-cost visual synchronization, a real fire dataset across 17 scenes, and synthetic fire scenes with ground-truth velocity fields.

The experimental evidence is fairly broad. The method is compared against several relevant Gaussian-splatting baselines, including 4DGS variants, Grid4D, and FreeTimeGS, and it improves visual metrics, masked flame metrics, depth plausibility, video quality, and synthetic velocity-field metrics.

The evaluation goes beyond frame-level PSNR/SSIM by considering depth consistency, temporal/video quality, and physically meaningful motion via the proposed density-weighted volumetric evaluation protocol. This is important because visual frame metrics alone can hide degenerate 3D or temporal behavior.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with useful supplementary details about capture, rolling shutter, dataset composition, implementation, runtime, and per-scene results. The limitations section is meaningful and acknowledges optical-flow errors, linear-motion simplifications, foreground/background separation assumptions, and residual synchronization artifacts.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than transformative. Several ingredients are adapted from existing 3DGS, FreeTimeGS-style temporal Gaussians, COLMAP/PatchMatch/depth priors, and optical flow. The main contribution is an effective integration for fire rather than a broadly new representation or optimization principle.

The evaluation scope is specialized. Results are strong for fire captured in a controlled three-camera setup, but it remains unclear how well the approach generalizes to smoke-heavy scenes, larger outdoor fires, reflective/complex backgrounds, stronger lighting changes, or fewer/more casually placed cameras.

The synchronization ablation is not fully convincing as a justification for the custom hardware: NoSync has almost identical real-world image/depth metrics and only modest synthetic degradation. The paper should better clarify when precise synchronization is essential and whether the added hardware complexity is necessary in typical use.

Some metrics rely on imperfect proxies. Real-scene flame depth is evaluated against aligned monocular depth predictions rather than true depth, and motion accuracy is evaluated only on synthetic scenes. These are reasonable choices for the domain, but they leave residual uncertainty about real-world 3D/velocity correctness.

The baseline comparison may be somewhat sensitive to initialization and tuning. Most baselines use author-provided settings for a different dynamic-scene case, and FreeTimeGS uses an unofficial implementation. The paper argues these methods fail fundamentally, but stronger per-baseline tuning or additional ablations would make the claim more robust.

The method still depends heavily on dense optical flow and motion masks, both of which are known to be fragile for flames because of transparency, rapid intensity changes, and weak texture. The limitations mention this, but the experiments do not deeply characterize failure modes as flow quality degrades.

Reproducibility is promising because code/data are promised, but the manuscript currently leaves the repository blank in the supplementary section. Important practical details such as exact voxel size selection, mask generation parameters, synchronization decoding robustness, and hyperparameter sensitivity could be more explicit.
